bodyEn: The poet Jorge Luis Borges wrote a famous short story about a society that had become so good at making maps, so obsessed with capturing every detail, that its rulers decided the only way to do the job right was to make a lifesize map of its entire empire, which could then be laid out across the actual land from coast to coast. Imagine a map of Britain the exact same size as Britain, showing every branch of Greggs, every nail bar, every vape shop in perfect detail. Only then can we really see what Britain looks like, by standing on a fake Britain laid over the top of actual Britain.

Borges was writing in the 1940s, at a time when people were fascinated by the mechanised future, with its new forms of measuring out the world: the wireless, the 30mph motorcar, the rise of Big Tape Measure. And to be fair, the mega-map is a pretty accurate vision of our own fully networked present, a place where you can snoop around a village in Mozambique from your laptop in Egham, where no one ever stops committing acts of minute self-surveillance, even if they think they’re just searching “What is beetroot?” on the internet.

Borges also hated football. “Soccer is popular because stupidity is popular,” he wrote, which probably seemed a bold statement at the time. But then Borges also didn’t live to see an episode of Wow Sports Premier League Breakfast at Breakfast with Roger McRoger and a puzzled Lee Trundle. After which, perhaps less of a surprise. But the process he describes is also a good description of what football is doing to itself. Endless data, endless analysis, no spaces or free air, matches that are just schematised movement. At times it can feel like football is out there laying a lifesize real-time map on top of itself.

In Borges’s story, the land soon begins to decay beneath the massive map – which is reassessed by later generations as insane, pointless and stupid – and left to rot in the desert. We haven’t reached this point. Nobody is de-mapping football. But it does perhaps explain why everyone gets so excited when a talent emerges that seems to be playful and human, to exist outside the grid. And also why it has felt wrong to gush too soon about Max Dowman, to fear placing the hex on him. We know how this works. Here is a fluffy new thing. Let us break him. Let us heap pressure on his shoulders. Don’t talk about Max Dowman. Let Max Dowman exist, breathe, bloom in the shadows.

So, Max Dowman then. It has become quite hard to ignore him. He was brilliant against Ipswich in midweek, and brilliant in a way that seems solid and real and comfortable with itself. Most obviously there were the two goals, both a perfect snapshot of why Dowman seems equipped to survive, more state‑of‑the‑art than some other young players we’ve burdened with expectation.

The second goal is particularly good, five perfect little actions packed into six seconds of football. Arsenal have the ball on the edge of the Ipswich box. Dowman shows for a pass, sees it’s going elsewhere, changes his mind, and makes a three-yard sprint to create space. Finally he has the physical capacity to control a bouncing ball in that sliver of space, to move his feet so much quicker than the nearest defender it looks like a glitch in the machine, and to finish in a way that involves sifting the options and timing the shot, all without breaking stride.

The first goal is on his other side, and involves a more classical piece of one-on-one deception. This is the same defender: Cédric Kipré, 29 years old, came through Paris Saint-Germain’s youth system. Dowman walks through him with a micro-feint and a switch of feet, then reels off another hilariously understated finish, doing it all while a second defender is still gathering himself to lunge, like a man operating in a different time signature to everyone around him.

This is the key point of difference, the ability to make everything stop, the fly-vision that means he sees what’s about to happen while everyone else is whirling about trying to read the charts, in the same way Lionel Messi (yes, sorry, sorry) always seems to have time to pass the ball into the net, like this is all a kickabout in a pair of sliders.

Our way of understanding young creative players has often seemed to lag behind where the game actually is, to be driven by nostalgia for what this thing used to look like. I remember the excitement over the 18-year-old Jack Rodwell’s physicality at the exact moment physicality was no longer going to be a thing, like proudly unveiling the latest horse‑drawn train just as the Ford Model T rolls off the production line.

Michael Owen was brilliant at 17, but he was mainly brilliant at running very fast in a straight line and smashing the ball into the net. Plus of course there was Wayne Rooney, who emerged a pale, unformed teenager composed entirely from energy drinks and white bread, out there making the game up on the fly, as though some urban foundling had come barrelling over the advert boards with a string of sausages still dangling from his mouth.

The narrative around Rooney is that he lost this vital native quality. But Rooney adapted and survived, and clearly understood what he had to be a lot better than those of us watching. And even now creative players have to exist against this. Cole Palmer is exciting because he does surprising things that seem to be striking a blow for freedom, beauty and older people who struggle to make their email work. But his real challenge is to retain just enough of this while fitting the world around him.

Dowman is a bit different. The things that make him stand out seem to speak very easily to how football is now. Being a modern creative footballer is not jinking runs, rasping drives or dribbling across a cabbage field in a pair of cowboy boots. It’s targeted energy, high-intensity semi-freedom. Lamine Yamal and Désiré Doué have the same fast-twitch foot and brain speed, the ability to operate in micro-moments, to see patterns just ahead of time. Dowman is 6ft tall and getting stronger. He won’t be kicked to pieces. He can repeat this without taking bites out of himself.

There is still the issue of his youth. But maybe this doesn’t matter so much either. The world has changed. In the age of Rooney and Owen there was no care, no data, no softness. This is where the structures of modern football are an advantage. Dowman will be GPS’d to the last decimal point. Endless physical scientists will have a say on his output and stress levels.

The money is too big. The talent is too valuable. It also comes ready to plug and play. You don’t get to this level unless you can ingest systems and briefings. You’ve already been pressure-cooked and stress-tested. What you’re being asked to do in the orderly spaces of professional football is the same thing you were asked to do in the orderly spaces of academy football, just five levels up and with more people watching.

Borges was anti-football because he saw it as inauthentic, the players no longer sports people but “actors in jerseys before the TV cameras”. And this is also fine, further evidence that boomer-dad nostalgia is one of the key archetypes of human behaviour.

Life is also different now; not harder or easier, but more instant, a series of moments, the creation of rapid-fire energy. Dowman has grown up inside this. He can parcel his time out, disappear for a bit, maybe make a show of things in the spring.

And yes, this is another way of fitting him to a model, laying a lifesize map of future Max Dowman across the present. But I strongly suspect he will be fine, and that unlike so many other things out there he’s pretty well adapted to whatever the future is supposed to look like.
items.author: Barney Ronay
items.titleZh: 我们本想让马克斯·道曼在阴影中绽放，但他如今已让人难以忽视
items.summaryZh: 阿森纳小将马克斯·道曼表现出色，展现出适应现代足球的巨大潜力。
bodyZh: 诗人豪尔赫·路易斯·博尔赫斯曾写过一篇著名的短篇小说，讲述了一个极其擅长绘制地图、痴迷于捕捉每一个细节的社会，其统治者认为把工作做好的唯一方法就是绘制一张与整个帝国等大的地图，然后将其铺在从海岸到海岸的实际土地上。想象一下一张与英国大小完全相同的英国地图，以完美的细节显示了格雷格斯的每一家分店、每一家美甲店、每一家电子烟店。只有这样，通过站在覆盖在真实英国之上的虚假英国上，我们才能真正看到英国是什么样子的。
博尔赫斯写作于20世纪40年代，当时人们对机械化的未来及其衡量世界的新方式着迷：无线电设备、时速30英里的汽车、巨型卷尺的兴起。平心而论，超级地图确实是我们现在这个完全联网的时代的精准愿景，在这里你可以通过英厄姆的笔记本电脑窥探莫桑比克的一个村庄，在这里没有人会停止进行微观的自我监视，即使他们认为自己只是在互联网上搜索“什么是甜菜根”。

博尔赫斯也讨厌足球。“足球受欢迎是因为愚蠢受欢迎，”他写道，这在当时可能是一个很大胆的说法。但博尔赫斯也没有活到看到罗杰·麦克罗杰和困惑的李·特伦德主持的《疯狂体育英超早餐》节目的那一刻。在那之后，也许就不会那么令人惊讶了。但他所描述的过程也是足球对其自身所做事情的生动写照。无休止的数据、无休止的分析、没有空间或自由空气、比赛只是图解式的运动。有时人们会觉得足球正在把一张与现实等时的地图铺在自己身上。

在博尔赫斯的故事中，巨大的地图之下的土地很快就开始腐烂——后来几代人重新评估其为疯狂、毫无意义和愚蠢——并任其在沙漠中腐烂。我们还没有到达这一点。没有人会取消足球的地图化。但这也许可以解释为什么当一个看起来俏皮、有人情味且存在于网格之外的天才涌现时，每个人都会如此兴奋。这也解释了为什么过早对马克斯·道曼大加赞赏会让人感觉不对劲，并担心给他带来魔咒。我们知道这是怎么回事。这是一个毛茸茸的新东西。让我们摧毁他。让我们把压力压在他的肩膀上。不要谈论马克斯·道曼。让马克斯·道曼存在、呼吸并在阴影中绽放。
那么，说说马克斯·道曼吧。现在要忽视他变得相当困难。他在周中的比赛中对阵伊普斯威奇时表现出色，这种出色显得扎实、真实且内心笃定。最明显的是那两个进球，这两个进球都是完美的快照，解释了为什么道曼似乎具备生存的能力，比我们赋予期望的其他一些年轻球员更具现代感。
第二个进球格外精彩，在六秒钟的足球比赛中包含了五个完美的微小动作。阿森纳在伊普斯威奇禁区边缘控球。道曼寻求传球，发现球传向别处，改变了主意，并进行了三码的冲刺来创造空间。最终，他在那个狭小的空间里具备了控制弹地球的身体能力，其挪动双脚的速度比最近的防守球员快得多，看起来就像机器出了故障，并且能够通过筛选选项和掌握射门时机的方式完成破门，而且全程步伐没有丝毫停顿。
第一个进球在她的另一侧，涉及更经典的一对一欺骗。这是同一名防守球员：塞德里克·基普雷，29岁，出自巴黎圣日耳曼青训营。道曼通过一次微假动作和脚法切换轻松过掉了他，随后又完成了一次令人捧腹的低调射门，这一切发生时，第二名防守球员还在调整身体准备扑抢，就像一个在与周围所有人处于不同时空节奏中运作的人。
这是关键的区别所在，这种让一切都停下来的能力，这种飞行般的视野意味着当其他所有人都在疯狂旋转试图解读图表时，他能看到即将发生的事情，就像莱昂内尔·梅西（是的，对不起，对不起）总是似乎有时间把球传进球门一样，就好像这一切只是穿着拖鞋在踢野球一样。
我们理解年轻创造型球员的方式似乎总是滞后于比赛的实际现状，并受到对过去事物怀旧情绪的驱使。我记得当18岁的杰克·罗德威尔的身体素质在身体素质不再重要的那一刻引发轰动时，就像在福特T型车刚下生产线时自豪地展示最新的马车火车一样。
迈克尔·欧文在17岁时就非常出色，但他主要的出色之处在于直线跑得非常快并将球轰入球网。当然还有韦恩·鲁尼，他作为一个面色苍白、尚未成型的青少年出现，完全由能量饮料和白面包组成，在场上即兴发挥，就像某种城市弃儿嘴里还叼着一串香肠越过广告牌狂奔而来一样。
围绕鲁尼的叙事是他失去了这种至关重要的本土特质。但鲁尼适应并生存了下来，并且显然比我们这些旁观者更清楚他必须成为什么样的人。即使在现在，创造型球员也必须在这种环境下生存。科尔·帕尔默令人兴奋，因为他做出了令人惊讶的事情，似乎在为自由、美以及那些电子邮件运行困难的老年人进行抗争。但他真正的挑战是在适应周围世界的同时，保留足够多的这种特质。
道曼则有些不同。让他脱颖而出的特质似乎非常契合现代足球的发展方向。现代创造型足球运动员不是花哨的盘带、刺耳的抽射，也不是穿着牛仔靴在菜地里盘带。而是有针对性的能量、高强度的半自由。亚马尔和杜埃拥有相同的快速应变脚法和头脑速度，具备在微观时刻运作的能力，能够在稍早前看到比赛的规律。道曼身高六英尺，而且身体变得更强壮了。他不会被踢得支离破碎。他可以重复这一点而不会消耗自己。
年轻仍然是个问题。但也许这也不是那么重要。世界已经变了。在鲁尼和欧文的时代，没有关怀，没有数据，没有温情。这就是现代足球结构发挥优势的地方。道曼将被精确到小数点后最后一位的GPS定位。无休止的体能科学家将对他的输出和压力水平发表意见。
资金太庞大了。天赋太宝贵了。它也做好了即插即用的准备。你若不具备吸收战术体系和简报的能力，就无法达到这个水平。你已经被高压烹调和压力测试过了。在职业足球有序的空间里被要求做的事情，和你在学院足球有序的空间里被要求做的事情是一样的，只是级别更高，有更多的人在观看。
博尔赫斯反足球是因为他认为足球是不真实的，球员不再是运动员，而是“电视摄像机前的球衣演员”。这也是可以理解的，这进一步证明了嬉皮士老爸式的怀旧是人类行为的关键原型之一。
生活现在也不同了；不是更难或更容易，而是更加瞬息万变，是一系列瞬间，是快速爆发能量的创造。道曼就是在这种环境下长大的。他可以分配自己的时间，消失一会儿，也许在春天大显身手。
是的，这也是将他纳入某种模版、将未来马克斯·道曼的等大地图铺在现实之上的另一种方式。但我坚信他会没事的，与外界许多其他事物不同，他非常适应未来的模样。

This season has continued the divergence between the clubs’ respective approaches, Brentford’s solidity and continuity contrasting with Chelsea attempting their latest reboot. Kevin Schade, after two well-taken goals at Bournemouth, will fancy facing a defence not yet attuned to Xabi Alonso’s configurations. Only one team has won a Premier League title with a defensive trio: Chelsea’s last title team, in 2016-17 under Antonio Conte. Alonso’s attack has been rather more successful, presenting another challenge for Jannik Schuster. Replacing Nathan Collins, the 20-year-old central defender had a tough examination from Bournemouth’s Evanilson on his first Premier League start, emerging with credit. For Chelsea, João Pedro has three goals and three assists, but doubts surrounding his fitness could lead to Danny Welbeck’s first league start. John Brewin
Brentford v Chelsea, Friday 8pm (all times BST)

What happens when a very stoppable force meets an extremely movable object? We will be tuning into events at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Saturday to find out as 19th-placed Aston Villa arrive in north London. The teams have scored one goal between them in the league and are desperately hoping for a first Premier League win. The return of Pedro Porro is big for Roberto De Zerbi and that should bring the Archie Gray Experiment at right-back to a merciful end. No Premier League starting XI feels less settled than Spurs – most players look as if they are a mistake or two from being dropped – which has culminated in a side that seems governed by fear and continuously prefers to take the safe option. After coming off the bench against Everton and Liverpool in the past week, the injury-plagued James Maddison will be itching to start and take some sort of initiative for Tottenham. Michael Butler
Tottenham v Aston Villa, Saturday 12.30pm

When Fabian Hürzeler spoke about Brighton’s success being founded on them being “well structured” after their stirring comeback against Manchester United at Old Trafford on Wednesday, he could have been referring to Malick Yalcouyé. The 20-year-old Ivorian moved to the south coast in 2024 after spending just a few months with IFK Gothenburg in Sweden but had to wait until this season to make his senior debut for Brighton after being sent on loan to Sturm Graz in Austria and then Swansea last season. With Jack Hinshelwood sidelined by injury until after the international break, Yalcouyé has taken his chance in the No 10 role and already found the net twice in the Premier League as Brighton have made a brilliant start. Arsenal are up next for the division’s top scorers – who have 13 goals from their opening four matches – and Mikel Arteta should be wary of the threat posed by Yalcouyé and co as the champions prepare for a fourth away game in succession. Ed Aarons
Brighton v Arsenal, Saturday 3pm

Vitalii Mykolenko’s early-season improvement has gone largely unheralded – and it probably always will be among his detractors – but at a time when David Moyes needs experienced players to step up and defy the constraints of a small squad, the Everton left-back has produced. Having signed a new three-year contract in the summer, and seemingly bulked up, the Ukraine international has kept his critics quiet with several impressive displays for a defence that has four clean sheets in six matches. There remains a problematic lack of cover at left-back after the decision to loan Adam Aznou to Málaga for the season but Mykolenko, the better defender, has eased the concerns that surrounded his position before the new campaign. Ipswich’s new forward recruits, Emersonn and Zian Flemming, will test Everton’s solidity but Moyes’s side will have made an encouraging start should they sign off with a win before the extended international break. Andy Hunter
Everton v Ipswich, Saturday 3pm

As befits a lover of direct football, Matthias Jaissle likes to get straight to the point. On Thursday he was asked whether, in the light of Monday night’s 4-1 thrashing at Leeds and a raft of injuries, he was tempted to perhaps switch to a back five or modify his beloved “vertical” approach when Hull visit Tyneside on Saturday. The reply proved unequivocal. “No,” said a manager unafraid to answer questions with a single word. Instead Jaissle expects his young team to retain faith in a wider vision as Newcastle – who signed eight players aged 24 and under this summer – adapt to life after Bruno Guimarães, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon. “It’s a brave journey the club is going on and I’m fully committed in that,” the German said. “If there’s one setback, we shouldn’t delete our journey or our vision. We’re fully committed. We’re fully aligned. We anticipated that something like that against Leeds would happen. It’s on us to respond. But while still believing. We don’t change.” Louise Taylor
Newcastle v Hull, Saturday 3pm

Many scoffed at the £45m that was paid for Liam Delap in the summer but Nottingham Forest feels like the perfect place for the striker to regain his form. Forest previously thrived with the now injured Chris Wood as their arrowhead and Delap is something of a younger regent for the New Zealander – powerful, instinctive and willing to bring others into play. During Saturday’s win at Villa, Morgan Gibbs-White and Delap looked as if they already have an understanding and both will be keen to capitalise against a Coventry side that have conceded eight goals in the past two games. After a nervy campaign last season, Forest feel back in the ascendancy and will have been delighted that plans to increase the City Ground’s capacity from 31,000 to 52,500, at an estimated cost of £790m, were approved by the local council on Wednesday. MB
Nottingham Forest v Coventry, Saturday 5.30pm

After watching Bournemouth make their European bow from afar in San Sebastián, a city Andoni Iraola knows inside out, the Basque head coach will return to his previous club on Sunday. Iraola – whose assistants Tommy Elphick and Shaun Cooper played for Bournemouth, the former captaining the club into the Premier League in 2015 – led the Dorset club into the Europa League by recording their best-ever finish, sixth. His body of work on the south coast earned him the Liverpool opportunity and a warm welcome is a guarantee. Despite the Cherries’ slow start under Iraola’s successor, Marco Rose, they will pose tricky opposition. The German spent a couple of hours in Iraola’s company before officially starting in June and both will be braced for an all-action contest. Eddie Howe failed to beat Bournemouth in the eight league games he managed against them with Newcastle and Iraola and his staff will expect a tough test. Ben Fisher
Bournemouth v Liverpool, Sunday 2pm

Dominic Calvert-Lewin will be a man on a mission against Crystal Palace at Elland Road on Saturday. Daniel Farke’s centre-forward hopes to become the first Leeds player to score in six consecutive home league games since Arthur Hydes back in 1932. Managers often, quite rightly, say players matter more than formations but, in Calvert-Lewin’s case, Farke’s switch to 3-5-2 late last November proved a road to Damascus moment. Until then he had struggled as the team’s lone striker but, once he was paired with Noah Okafor or Lukas Nmecha, the goals started to flow. Granted, Leeds sometimes play 3-4-3 or, occasionally, revert to a back four but Calvert-Lewin has emphasised the importance of attacking partnerships. After collecting eight points from their opening four games, Farke’s team have registered the best beginning to a top-tier campaign of any Leeds team since David O’Leary’s class of 2001-02. Will it continue at Palace’s expense? Is Hydes’ record under threat? Might 3-5-2 be the answer to ending more strikers’ goal droughts? Louise Taylor
Leeds v Crystal Palace, Sunday 2pm

Manchester City’s maximum 12 points from their first four Premier League games featured 1-0 wins (over Coventry and Manchester United), a 2-1 victory (Bournemouth), and a 4-1 success (Crystal Palace). Conceding only two goals while scoring eight is an impressive record that is only marginally bettered by the champions, Arsenal (one conceded, eight scored in their 12-point tally), and it seems a rosy augury that Enzo Maresca’s team will be genuine title contenders this season. Régis Le Bris, though, plots to halt City’s perfect start, and can draw on guiding Sunderland to a share of the points last season against the FA Cup holders, though that was at the Stadium of Light. In the corresponding fixture at the Etihad Stadium, City cruised to a 3-0 win. Jamie Jackson
Manchester City v Sunderland, Sunday 2pm

Oscar Bobb came off the bench against West Ham and fired Fulham into the fourth round of the Carabao Cup with a clinical late winner at the London Stadium on Tuesday night. It was a fine piece of individual play from the Norway winger but he needs to do it more often. The goal was Bobb’s first since joining Fulham last January and a player of his ability should be producing more of an end product. The 23-year-old is a clever dribbler and looked ready to establish himself at Manchester City before a serious injury curtailed his development. The talent is clear. Bobb had a good World Cup and should be full of confidence when Fulham, still seeking their first win in the league this season, host Manchester United. Jacob Steinberg
Fulham v Manchester United, Sunday 4.30pm

items.titleEn: A playground full of Lionesses by Lotte Wubben-Moy
items.summaryEn: After winning the Euros with the Lionesses, Lotte Wubben-Moy knew they needed to secure a legacy for girls in sport
bodyEn: After winning the Euros with the Lionesses, Lotte Wubben-Moy knew that more needed to be done in order to secure a sporting legacy for young girls in the UK.

Lotte and her fellow Lionesses wrote to the UK government asking to improve opportunities for girls to play football at school and this International Women's Day, the government has pledged that all schoolgirls will have equal access to football and sport.
Here is Lotte's open letter, reflecting on this achievement and what it means for the future:

When I was seven I would walk in the door from school and immediately leave again to go and play football in the street. I would simply shout downstairs to my mum that I was off out to play and fly out the door. She knew where I was, two streets over in our small neighbourhood in Bow. I would always return a couple of hours later, five friends and two grazed knees the richer.

I look back and can’t help but think how lucky I was to have found my place growing up. Football was part of my identity, it helped me find a clear path in one of the biggest cities in the world. I think I’d have been pretty lost without it. I learnt so much about the complexities of modern society and of the person I would become, during those games in the streets. The jostling for who would play in goal, what was defined as a foul (and what often wasn’t), and the fighting for my place. I grew in confidence and motivation to constantly improve and it was incredibly empowering to hold my own against all the boys (not that I would have ever considered that at the time).

I do however remember thinking ‘all the other girls in the local area are crazy not to join in playing with us. I couldn’t understand it. Why didn’t they want to earn the respect of other local kids our age? Or have the chance to make friends with kids from all over the area? In hindsight, I am sure many girls would have walked past us wishing they had the confidence to play along too.

Stories of battling to play reverberate around our Lionesses changing room: from playing in boys' teams to starting up our own teams, to travelling continents to find adequate girls' coaching, this was an experience many of us have lived and a battle we have all fought. It has shaped us, but we want better for the future.

Football has given me so much and I feel indebted to ensure it gives as much, if not more, to others. And that is exactly why we 23-Lionesses put pen to paper, writing to the Prime Minister in demand of equality. We were determined to ensure every young girl across the nation has equal access to football when they go to school. To ensure that our European Championship win could leave a legacy past last summer’s blurry few days of celebration and hoarsely singing "It's coming home" in Trafalgar square.

I never for one moment thought it was possible to become a professional footballer all those years ago. No sooner would I have believed you if you’d said I’d be writing letters to the Prime Minister. But I’m part of a generation who knows no end to our dreams. We dreamt of becoming European champions. We harbour dreams for this summer’s World Cup. And we also dream of a time when girls watch the WSL on a Sunday afternoon and run into school on a Monday morning ready for their shooting drills, emulating their heroes, dreaming themselves, and dreaming with no limits.
This is another victory we now believe we have achieved. And perhaps it will grow to become our greatest ever victory. We will do everything in our power to ensure that this is the case.

As I grew up the street was traded for real pitches. The football teams I was part of moved predominantly outside of the M25. This meant that the once-post-school run around the corner was replaced by an ever-growing dependence on my privilege; my mum would drive me to training three or four times a week, often taking along other girls from the local area with us. We could afford the many and frequent team payments, new boots, and match fees. And most importantly I always had my parents’ full support.

But I know there will be so many girls out there who are not so lucky. Having witnessed it first hand, I know this necessity to travel has already ended so many young players’ careers in London and perhaps stopped many more from ever beginning. This is one of the reasons I so strongly believe in the need for girls’ football at every school across the nation.

Our letter and lobbying reached the ears of those most powerful within the country. As of today's news from Number 10, millions of girls in schools across the nation will now finally have equal access to football at school. They will be able to do what their male classmates have been able to do for years: play football at school.

Picture a playground full of young girls kicking footballs around in London and pick out a future Lauren James. A playground in Cumbria, pick out that future Georgia Stanway. A playground in Wigan, who is the future Ella Toone? Imagine how many future Lionesses you could pick out in every playground across the nation with every school now offering equal access to football.

Well, that is now the reality the Lionesses squad of 2022 dreamt of. But the victory is so much greater than that, because many don’t play football dreaming of a professional career. It's the camaraderie, the adrenaline, and the endorphins that I felt as a young girl. It is the teamwork, the social networking, and the lifelong friends made on the pitch. It is the beautiful game, that I know so well.

By making girls' football more accessible, we have opened a crucial door for the growth of women’s football as a whole. And if we want to look at our Lionesses and see a team that represents the whole nation, I believe this is one among many key steps to ensuring our national team becomes more diverse, stronger, and more successful many years into the future.
Long live street football. I’ll forever be indebted.
Let Girls Play,
LWM

items.titleZh: 拉特·乌本-莫伊：充满女狮子们的操场
items.summaryZh: 乌本-莫伊谈推动英国校园女孩足球平权及未来愿景。
bodyZh: 随英格兰女足赢得欧洲杯后，阿森纳球员拉特·乌本-莫伊深知需要为英国年轻女孩的体育传承做更多事情。
拉特和队友们曾致信英国政府，要求改善女孩在学校踢球的机会。在这个国际妇女节，政府已承诺所有女校学生将平等获得踢足球和进行体育运动的机会。
以下是拉特的公开信，回顾了这一成就及其对未来的意义：
当我七岁的时候，放学进门后会立刻再次出门，去街上踢足球。我只是在楼下对妈妈喊一声我要出去玩，然后飞奔出门。她知道我在哪里，就在我们位于博（Bow）的小社区里两条街外。几个小时后我总是会回来，多了五个朋友和两处擦伤。

回首过去，我不禁觉得自己能在成长过程中找到归属感是多么幸运。足球是我身份的一部分，它帮助我在世界最大城市之一找到了一条清晰的道路。我想如果没有它，我会感到非常迷茫。在街头踢球的那些日子里，我学到了很多关于现代社会复杂性以及我将成为怎样的人的知识。关于谁来守门、什么是犯规（通常什么不是）以及争夺自己位置的争论。我的自信心和不断进步的动力都增强了，在所有男孩面前坚持自我（当时我从未这样想过）赋予了我难以置信的力量。
然而我确实记得当时想过：当地所有的其他女孩不加入我们踢球真是太疯狂了。我无法理解。为什么她们不想赢得我们这个年龄段其他本地孩子的尊重？或者没有机会结识来自全区各地的孩子？事后看来，我确信许多女孩走过我们身边时，都希望自己也有勇气一起踢球。
关于争取踢球机会的故事在我们的女狮子更衣室里回响：从在男孩球队踢球到自己组队，再到跨越大洲寻找合适的女孩教练，这是我们许多人经历过并共同抗争的战斗。它塑造了我们，但我们希望未来能变得更好。
足球给予了我太多，我感到责无旁贷，必须确保它给其他人带来同样多、甚至更多的东西。这正是我们23名女狮子付诸笔端、致信首相要求平权的原因。我们决心确保全国每个年轻女孩在学校时都能平等地踢足球。确保我们赢得的欧洲杯能够留下一份传承，超越去年夏天在特拉法加广场庆祝的模糊几天和嘶哑高歌的“足球回家”。
多年前我从未想过自己有可能成为一名职业足球运动员。如果你当时说我会给首相写信，我同样不会相信。但我属于这样一代人，我们的梦想永无止境。我们梦想成为欧洲冠军。我们怀揣着今年夏天世界杯的梦想。我们也梦想着这样一个时代：女孩们在周日下午观看女子英超联赛，周一早晨带着对英雄的模仿跑进校园准备射门训练，她们自己做梦，且梦想没有极限。
这是我们现在相信已经实现的又一场胜利。也许它会成长为我们有史以来最伟大的胜利。我们将尽一切努力确保实现这一目标。
随着我长大，街头换成了真正的球场。我所在的球队主要转移到了M25公路以外。这意味着曾经放学后在转角处的奔跑被逐渐增加的特权所取代：妈妈每周会开车送我去训练三四次，通常还会带上当地的其他女孩。我们负担得起频繁的球队费用、新球鞋和比赛费用。最重要的是，我始终得到了父母的全力支持。
但我知道会有很多女孩没有那么幸运。亲眼目睹后，我知道这种必须出行的需求已经结束了伦敦许多年轻球员的职业生涯，或许也阻碍了更多人的开始。这也是我坚信全国每所学校都需要开展女孩足球的原因之一。
我们的信件和游说传到了国内最具权势者的耳中。根据今天首相府发布的消息，全国学校数以百万计的女孩现在终于可以平等地在学校踢足球了。她们将能够做她们的男同学多年来一直能做的事情：在学校踢足球。
想象一个满是年轻女孩在伦敦踢球的操场，挑选出一个未来的劳伦·詹姆斯。一个在坎布里亚郡的操场，挑选出未来的乔治娅·斯坦韦。一个在威igan的操场，未来的埃拉·图恩是谁？想象一下，随着每所学校现在都提供平等的踢足球机会，你可以在全国每个操场挑选出多少未来的女狮子。
好吧，这就是2022年女狮子阵容梦想的现实。但这胜利远比这更伟大，因为许多人踢球并非为了梦想职业生涯。那是我年轻时感受到的友情、肾上腺素和内啡肽。这是团队合作、社交网络以及在球场上结下的终身友谊。这是我如此熟悉的精彩足球。
通过让女孩足球更加普及，我们为整个女子足球的发展打开了一扇至关重要的门。如果我们想看到我们的女狮子代表整个国家，我相信这是确保我们的国家队在未来许多年变得更加多元、强大和成功众多关键步骤中的一步。
街头足球万岁。我永远心怀感激。
让女孩们踢球吧，
LWM
